This article gives R code for the worked examples of the book *Experimental Design and Analysis for Tree
Improvement* (Williams, Harwood and Matheson, 2024). The data sets come with the package
[eda4treeR](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=eda4treeR) (Yaseen et al., 2023). Each example follows the
book: the data, the model, a check of the residuals, the analysis of variance and the predicted means with
their pairwise comparisons, computed with predictmeans. Section titles give the book's example number and
page. Where the analysis here differs from the book's, the text says why. The code of each step is folded:
click **Code** to see it.

Mixed models are fitted with `lme4::lmer()` (attached with predictmeans). Their F tests (`anova()`) and
predicted means use Kenward-Roger standard errors and degrees of freedom, as SAS PROC MIXED `DDFM=KR`
(Kenward and Roger, 1997); variance components are from `varcomp()`.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(predictmeans)
library(eda4treeR)
library(gridExtra)
library(car)
library(DT)
library(gt)
library(summarytools)
library(knitr)
```


## **2.1 Example 2.1 (Pg. 24)**

A field trial was planted to compare a seedlot derived from a seed orchard (SO) with one collected from a routine plantation (P). There were eight plots of each seedlot, thinned at seven years of age. Tree diameters at breast height (dbh) were measured at 15 years and plot means calculated.

### Data Info {.tabset .tabset-pills}

#### Structure

```{r}
data(DataExam2.1, package="eda4treeR")
str(DataExam2.1)
```
#### Summary
```{r}
print(dfSummary(DataExam2.1, 
                varnumbers   = FALSE, 
                valid.col    = FALSE, 
                graph.magnif = 0.76),
      method = 'render')
```

#### Plot

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7
DataExam2.1 %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=seedlot, y=dbh, col=seedlot, fill=seedlot))+
  geom_boxplot(width=0.3, alpha=0.4)+
  geom_jitter(size=2)+
  theme_bw(9)
```


### Modelling {.tabset .tabset-pills}

#### Model

```{r}
fmtab2.3 <- lm(formula = dbh ~ seedlot , data = DataExam2.1)
summary(fmtab2.3)
```

#### Residual Plot

```{r}
residplot(fmtab2.3) 
```

#### Test

```{r}
#perform shapiro-wilk test
shapiro.test(resid(fmtab2.3))

#perform bartlett test
bartlett.test(dbh ~ seedlot , data = DataExam2.1)

#perform levene test 
car::leveneTest(dbh ~ seedlot , data = DataExam2.1)
```


### ANOVA

```{r}
kable(anova(fmtab2.3), digits = 4)
```

### Predicted Means {.tabset .tabset-pills}


#### Mean Table

```{r}
#| fig.show: hide
predm_out <- predictmeans(fmtab2.3, "seedlot", meandecr=TRUE, adj="BH")
print(predm_out[1:4])
gt(predm_out$mean_table$Table, 
   caption = "Group: Letter-based representation of pairwise comparisons at significant level '0.05'")
```

#### Mean Plot

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7
autoplot(predm_out)
autoplot(predm_out, type = "ci", data = TRUE)
autoplot(predm_out, type = "bar")
```

## **3.1 Example 3.1 (Pg. 30)**

We illustrate the recommended layout for data sheets with one of the trials conducted by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in Queensland, Australia (Experiment 309). This was a species trial planted in 1985; survival was poor. For our example we will examine only part of the data from this experiment. Five of the species with good survival have been extracted at random, namely Acacia, Angophora, Casuarina, Melaleuca and Petalostigma.

### Data Info {.tabset .tabset-pills}

#### Structure

```{r}
data(DataExam3.1, package="eda4treeR")
str(DataExam3.1)
```

#### Summary
```{r}
print(dfSummary(DataExam3.1, 
                varnumbers   = FALSE, 
                valid.col    = FALSE, 
                graph.magnif = 0.76),
      method = 'render')
```


### Modelling {.tabset .tabset-pills}

#### Model

```{r}
fmtab3.3 <- aov(ht ~ Error(repl/PlotNo)+seedlot, data = DataExam3.1)
summary(fmtab3.3)
```

#### Residual Plot

```{r}
residplot(fmtab3.3) 
```


### Predicted Means {.tabset .tabset-pills}

#### Mean Table

-   Mean
```{r}
#| fig.show: hide
predm_out <- predictmeans(fmtab3.3, "seedlot", adj="BH")
print(predm_out[1:4])
gt(predm_out$mean_table$Table, 
   caption = "Group: Letter-based representation of pairwise comparisons at significant level '0.05'")
```

-   Pairwise p-values
```{r}
gt(data.frame(predm_out$`Pairwise p-value`, check.names=FALSE), 
   rownames_to_stub=TRUE, 
   caption = "The matrix has t-value above the diagonal, p-value (adjusted by 'BH' method) below the diagonal") %>% 
  cols_width(everything() ~ px(130))
```

#### Mean Plot

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7
autoplot(predm_out)
autoplot(predm_out, type = "ci", data = TRUE)
autoplot(predm_out, type = "bar")
```


### Remove three outliers

-   Outliers:
```{r}
DataExam3.1[c(28, 51, 76), ] %>% 
  gt(rownames_to_stub=TRUE)
```

-   Model:
```{r}
fmtab3.3N <- aov(ht ~ Error(repl/PlotNo/TreeNo)+seedlot, data = DataExam3.1[-c(28, 51, 76), ])
summary(fmtab3.3N)
```

## **4.1 Example 4.3 (Pg. 53)**

### Data Info {.tabset .tabset-pills}

Major seed distributors such as the Australian Tree Seed Centre (ATSC) routinely conduct seed viability tests so that, when seed is dispatched, the purchaser has an indication of the germination percentage of the seed. As part of the ATSC research program, a series of experiments was conducted in 1992 by Debbie Solomon on provenances of Acacia mangium to investigate methods of pre-treatment and loss of viability of stored seed. Each experiment involved six seedlots of Acacia mangium and four seed pre-treatments in a factorial design with three replicates.

#### Structure

```{r}
data(DataExam4.3, package="eda4treeR")
DataExam4.3$treat <- factor(DataExam4.3$treat, levels =c("control", "nick", "bw&s", "bw1min"))
DataExam4.3$contcomp <- factor(DataExam4.3$contcomp, levels = c("control", "Treated"))
str(DataExam4.3)
```

#### Summary

```{r}
print(dfSummary(DataExam4.3, 
                varnumbers   = FALSE, 
                valid.col    = FALSE, 
                graph.magnif = 0.76),
      method = 'render')
```


### Modelling {.tabset .tabset-pills}

#### Model

```{r}
fm4.2 <- aov(percent ~ repl + contcomp + seedlot +
               treat/contcomp + contcomp/seedlot + treat/contcomp/seedlot
             , data = DataExam4.3)
kable(anova(fm4.2), digits = 4) 
```

#### Residual Plot

```{r}
residplot(fm4.2) 
```

## **4.2 Example 4.4 (Pg. 61)**

### Data Info {.tabset .tabset-pills}

An experiment supported by the Shell Company was planted at Toolara Forest Reserve near Gympie, Queensland, in February 1987 to study the effects of irrigation and fertiliser on four seedlots of Eucalyptus grandis. Because of the difficulty in applying the irrigation and fertiliser treatments individually to each
7 × 6 plot of trees, the experiment was designed as a split-plot, with main-plot treatments, irrig and fert. There were two replicates of four main-plots each with four sub-plots.

#### Structure

```{r}
data(DataExam4.4, package="eda4treeR")
DataExam4.4$seedlot <- factor(as.character(DataExam4.4$seedlot))
str(DataExam4.4)
```

#### Summary

```{r}
print(dfSummary(DataExam4.4, 
                varnumbers   = FALSE, 
                valid.col    = FALSE, 
                graph.magnif = 0.76),
      method = 'render')
```


### Modelling {.tabset .tabset-pills}

#### Model

```{r}
fm4.6 <- aov(height ~ repl + irrig*fert*seedlot +
Error(repl/irrig:fert), data = DataExam4.4)
summary(fm4.6)
```

#### Residual Plot

```{r}
residplot(fm4.6) 
```

## **5.2 Example 5.1 (Pg. 68)**

### Data Info {.tabset .tabset-pills}

In 1985 species/provenance trials were laid out at six sites in Thailand as part of an ACIAR project extending over several years to investigate Australian multi-purpose tree species. The experimental design in each case was an RCB design with three replicates and the number of seedlots ranged from 30 to 42. Plots consisted of 5 × 5 trees with a 2m × 2m spacing. Plot summary files were constructed for the 24-month measurement according to the methods described in Chapter 3. Analyses were performed on the plot mean data at each site.

#### Structure

```{r}
data(DataExam5.1, package="eda4treeR")
str(DataExam5.1)
```

#### Summary

```{r}
print(dfSummary(DataExam5.1, 
                varnumbers   = FALSE, 
                valid.col    = FALSE, 
                graph.magnif = 0.76),
      method = 'render')
```


### Modelling

-   ANOVA
One value per site and seedlot (a plot mean), so the full model leaves no residual: its F tests are
empty (NaN) until the book's pooled residual mean square is added below.

```{r}
fm5.2 <- lm(ht ~ site*seedlot, DataExam5.1)
kable(anova(fm5.2), digits = 4) 
```

-   Predicted Means

Site:
```{r}
site_mean <- Kmatrix(fm5.2, "site")$K%*%coef(fm5.2)
site_df <- data.frame(Site=rownames(site_mean), Mean=site_mean)
gt(site_df)
```

Seedlot:
```{r}

gt(data.frame(seedlot_mean[, 1:9, drop=FALSE], check.names = FALSE, row.names ="Mean"), rownames_to_stub = TRUE)
gt(data.frame(seedlot_mean[, 10:18, drop=FALSE], check.names = FALSE, row.names ="Mean"), rownames_to_stub = TRUE)
gt(data.frame(seedlot_mean[, 19:27, drop=FALSE], check.names = FALSE, row.names ="Mean"), rownames_to_stub = TRUE)
```

-   Table of seedlot mean and regression coefficients

Site means absorb the main slope on `sitemean` (it is constant within a site), so the model estimates only
the differences between the seedlots' slopes (`sitemean:seedlot`). As in joint regression analysis, the
slopes are scaled to average 1. For this complete table they equal the book's Table 5.7.

```{r}
predm_seedlot <- predictmeans(mod_5.1, "seedlot", plot=FALSE)$mean_table
d <- c(0, coef(mod_5.1)[grep("^sitemean:seedlot", names(coef(mod_5.1)))])   # slope differences from the first seedlot
predm_seedlot$reg_coef <- 1 + d - mean(d)
gt(predm_seedlot)
```

-   Joint regression lines: each seedlot's line through its mean at the average site mean, with its slope.
    (`covariatemeans()` is not used: with `site` in the model, a seedlot mean at any other value of
    `sitemean` is not estimable.)
```{r}
xm <- mean(unique(DataExam5.1[c("site", "sitemean")])$sitemean)
ggplot(predm_seedlot) +
  geom_abline(aes(intercept = Mean - reg_coef*xm, slope = reg_coef), alpha = 0.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = range(DataExam5.1$sitemean)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = range(DataExam5.1$ht, na.rm = TRUE)) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Site mean", y = "Predicted height")
```


## **6.2 Example 6.2 (Pg. 94)**

### Data Info {.tabset .tabset-pills}

Open-pollinated families from three provenance regions (PNG, Sabah, Queensland), 48 families in four
replicates, one plot per family and replicate. The data are plot means of diameter (`Dbh.mean`) with the
variance among the trees of each plot (`Dbh.variance`) and their number (`Dbh.count`).

#### Structure

```{r}
data(DataExam6.2, package = "eda4treeR")
DataExam6.2.1 <- droplevels(subset(DataExam6.2, Province == "PNG"))
str(DataExam6.2)
```

#### Summary

```{r}
print(dfSummary(DataExam6.2,
                varnumbers   = FALSE,
                valid.col    = FALSE,
                graph.magnif = 0.76),
      method = 'render')
```

### Modelling {.tabset .tabset-pills}

#### Model (PNG families)

Families are random; replicates fixed.

```{r}
fm6.3.1 <- lmer(Dbh.mean ~ Replication + (1 | Family), data = DataExam6.2.1)
gt(varcomp(fm6.3.1), rownames_to_stub = TRUE)
```

#### Residual Plot

```{r}
residplot(fm6.3.1)
```

### Heritability {.tabset .tabset-pills}

#### Single tree (Pg. 104)

Narrow-sense heritability of a single tree: the additive variance is the family variance divided by the
coefficient of relationship among members of an open-pollinated family, taken as 0.3 in the book (between
half-sibs, 0.25, and full-sibs, 0.5). Plot means hold only 1/n of the variance among trees within a plot, so the
single-tree variance needs that variance (`within_variance`) and the number of trees per plot (`within_n`,
harmonic mean): \(\sigma^2_P = \sigma^2_f + \sigma^2_m + \sigma^2_w\), with plot variance
\(\sigma^2_m = \sigma^2_e - \sigma^2_w/n\).

```{r}
heritability(fm6.3.1, "Family", method = "family", relationship = 0.3,
             within_variance = "Dbh.variance", within_n = "Dbh.count")
```

#### Family means

The heritability of family means (the precision of the family ranking in this trial). The data are balanced,
so the standard, Cullis, Piepho and Oakey forms agree; the mean reliability is a little lower (it leaves out the
covariances of the prediction errors), and the simulated form differs by its Monte Carlo error (printed below
the table).

```{r}
heritability(fm6.3.1, "Family", method = "all", seed = 1)
```

#### All provenances (Pg. 107)

With all three provenances, provenance is a fixed effect, so the family variance is that within provenances.

```{r}
fm6.4.1 <- lmer(Dbh.mean ~ Replication + Province + (1 | Family), data = DataExam6.2)
gt(varcomp(fm6.4.1), rownames_to_stub = TRUE)
heritability(fm6.4.1, "Family", method = "family", relationship = 0.3,
             within_variance = "Dbh.variance", within_n = "Dbh.count")
```


## **8.1 Example 8.1 (Pg. 139)**

### Data Info {.tabset .tabset-pills}

In the early 1990s Khongsak Pinyopusarerk of CSIRO Forestry and Forest Products initiated a far-reaching study of Casuarina equisetifolia. This is a nitrogen-fixing tree of considerable social, economic and environmental importance in tropical/subtropical littoral zones of Asia, the Pacific and Africa. Provenance collections were obtained from 18 countries and, with this material, more than 40 trials were laid out in 20 countries. The number of seedlots included in each trial varied, depending on the suitability and size of the planting sites for the available material. One of the trials, in Weipa, northern Queensland, contained all the available seedlots and is the example used here.

#### Structure

```{r}
data(DataExam8.1, package="eda4treeR")
DataExam8.1$inoc <- factor(DataExam8.1$inoc, levels=c("1 week", "7 weeks"))
DataExam8.1$country <- factor(as.character(DataExam8.1$country))
str(DataExam8.1)
```

#### Summary

```{r}
print(dfSummary(DataExam8.1, 
                varnumbers   = FALSE, 
                valid.col    = FALSE, 
                graph.magnif = 0.76),
      method = 'render')
```


### Modelling {.tabset .tabset-pills}

#### Model

Inoculation was applied to whole replicates, so it is tested in the replicate stratum (2 df). Each
row-by-column position within a replicate is one plot, the residual unit, so `Error(repl)` gives the two
strata (`Error(repl/(row:col))` adds a stratum that is the residual itself). The means and SEDs below are
computed by strata and agree with Genstat.

```{r}
fm8.2 <- aov(dbh ~ inoc*(country/prov) + Error(repl), data = DataExam8.1)
summary(fm8.2)
```

#### Residual Plot

```{r}
residplot(fm8.2) 
```


### Predicted Means

-   inoc
```{r}
predm_out <- predictmeans(fm8.2, "inoc", plot=FALSE)
print(predm_out[1:4])
gt(predm_out$mean_table)
```

-   country
```{r}
predm_out <- predictmeans(fm8.2, "country", plot=FALSE)
print(predm_out[1:4])
gt(predm_out$mean_table)
```

```{r}

print(predm_out[1:4])
gt(predm_out$mean_table)
```

## **8.5 Example 8.2 (Pg. 157)**

### Data Info {.tabset .tabset-pills}

In Example 7.1 we discussed a Eucalyptus clone trial conducted in Vietnam and described the experimental layout. The trial tested 56 hybrid clones of the interspecific hybrid combination E. urophylla × E. pellita (UP). These candidates had been selected from progeny trials of control-pollinated hybrid families; here we ignore the parental origins of the different UP clones.

#### Structure

```{r}
data(DataExam8.2, package="eda4treeR")
DataExam8.2$standard <- factor(DataExam8.2$standard, levels=c("0", "PN14", "SSOseed", "U6", "UG323"))
str(DataExam8.2)
```

#### Summary

```{r}
print(dfSummary(DataExam8.2, 
                varnumbers   = FALSE, 
                valid.col    = FALSE, 
                graph.magnif = 0.76),
      method = 'render')
```


### Modelling {.tabset .tabset-pills}


#### Model

Clone effects are random for the test clones only (`contcompf` = 1); the four standards are fixed effects
(`contcompf:standard`). This is Genstat's `contcompv.clone` with `contcompv` = 1 for test clones and 0 for
standards. `(1 | contcompv:clone)` would instead add one more random "clone" holding all 20 standard plots
(their `clone` is `"0"`), confounded with the fixed `contcompf` effect: it changes the test of `contcompf`
(F 4.8 on 43 df instead of 73 on 255).

```{r}
fm8.7 <- lmer(dbh ~ repl + column + contcompf + contcompf:standard + (1 | repl:row) + (1 | repl:column) +
                (0 + dummy(contcompf, "1") | clone), data = DataExam8.2)
summary(fm8.7, corr=FALSE)
```

#### Residual Plot
```{r}
residplot(fm8.7)
```


### ANOVA, adjusted $R^2$, Varcomp

-   ANOVA

Sequential (Type I) tests with Kenward-Roger df, = SAS PROC MIXED (`HTYPE=1`, `DDFM=KR`). Genstat's
"sequentially adding terms" tests the same hypotheses for `repl` and `contcompf.standard` and different ones
for `column` and `contcompf`, because it builds them from the fitted variances; it also uses an F without
Kenward-Roger's adjustment (see `?anova.lmerMod`). Genstat's Wald and F statistics:

```{r}
kable(anova(fm8.7, type = 1), digits = 4)
kable(anova(fm8.7, type = 1, type1_basis = "fitted", ddf = "KR-average"), digits = 4)
```

-   Adjusted $R^2$
```{r}
R2_model(fm8.7)
```

-   Varcomp
```{r}
gt(varcomp(fm8.7), rownames_to_stub=TRUE)
```

### Predicted Means {.tabset .tabset-pills}

-   repl
```{r}
predictmeans(fm8.7, "repl", plot=FALSE)
```

-   column
```{r}
predictmeans(fm8.7, "column", plot=FALSE)
```

-   standard|contcompf


#### Mean
```{r}
predm_out <- predictmeans(fm8.7, "contcompf:standard", atvar="contcompf", plot=FALSE)
print(predm_out[1:4])
gt(predm_out$mean_table$Table, groupname_col = "contcompf")
```

#### Pairwise p-values
```{r}
gt(data.frame(predm_out$`Pairwise p-value`, check.names=FALSE), 
   rownames_to_stub=TRUE, 
   caption = "The matrix has t-value above the diagonal, p-value (adjusted by 'BH' method) below the diagonal") %>% 
  cols_width(everything() ~ px(120))
```
